citations.quote: Objectives: This paper provides a systematic literature review of DT applications in space robotics. The study aims to (i) classify primary objectives of their use, (ii) map applications across system lifecycle phases, (iii) identify recurring challenges, and (iv) report advantages while deriving analytical insights for future research.
RQ1: What are the primary objectives of using DTs in space robotics?
RQ2: What are the applications of DTs in space robotics?
RQ3: What are the current challenges and limitations of integrating DTs in space robotics?
RQ4: What are the advantages of using DTs in space robotics?

Building on these questions, our systematic literature review synthesizes the state of the art on DTs for space robotics by analyzing 46 peer-reviewed publications indexed in IEEE Xplore, ACM, and Scopus (covering studies up to the end of June 2024).

"Digital twin*" AND (("Aerospace" OR " Astronautical" OR "Spacecraft" OR "Space technology" OR "Space domain*" OR (" space exploration" OR "space mission*")) AND ("Robotic*" OR "Robot*")) OR ((" Rover*" OR "Perseverance" OR "Sojourner" OR "Spirit" OR "Curiosity")))
We covered all the studies from scratch till the end of June 2024.
Using this keyword, relevant papers were derived from the largest and most widely used scientific indexing systems and databases in software engineering: SCOPUS, IEEE Xplore Digital Library, and ACM.
These criteria were applied while reading the abstract and title of the articles. The articles that were identified outside the research domain did not proceed to the analysis stage.
IC1: Journal or conference publications with space applications.

citations.quote: only once, then, 1358 papers were left to initial check. In this stage, we exclude irrelevant studies by reading the titles and abstracts. At the end of this stage, 67 papers were left for meticulous review and analysis. The drastic decrease in the number of papers was caused by studies that only referenced the initial study of DT, which pertains to the aerospace domain, without further investigation. After filtering out in the final selection and conducting backward and forward snowballing search, 38 papers were discerned as directly related to the purpose of our study. We then conducted snowballing on the remaining papers to identify additional relevant studies. This process yielded 8 additional papers, bringing the total number of selected papers to 46.

To address the methodological rigor of the included studies, we conducted a structured quality assessment of each selected paper. The goal of this appraisal is to analyze the papers and to enable an evidence-based synthesis.

We assessed methodological reporting quality using the rubric in Table 3 and separately coded each study for objectives, lifecycle phase, modeling paradigm, validation realism, and deployment characteristics.

DT objectives in space robotics are mainly centered on assembly tasks and robot behavior modeling, reflecting a focus on measurable performance optimization and operational refinement. Conversely, usage targeting satellite communication and networking infrastructures, along with human-robot collaboration, is less represented.

DT applications in space robotics span the design, manufacturing, and service phases; however, they are unevenly distributed and predominantly phase-local. In the design phase, DTs are mainly used for iterative optimization and virtual verification of complex models. In manufacturing, they support production control, real-time monitoring, and quality management in smart assembly environments. In the service phase, DT implementations primarily focus on state monitoring, fault detection, and predictive maintenance.

They applied DT to monitor and control production processes, test different scenarios, optimize the assembly and integration of CubeSats before the actual physical implementation, provide data and bidirectional connection with the physical entity, detect faults, and enhance the robustness of the process.

Figueroa et al. [45] implemented a DT for the power manager system of the NASA Artemis Mission. They used the NASA Platform for Autonomous Systems electrical equipment domain libraries to create DT for fault diagnosis in the system.

In space exploration, DTs enhance the performance of rovers by detecting anomalies such as driving motors, solar panels, and electric heaters [44], assessing the degradation of spacecraft battery packs [55], and improving control strategies under realistic conditions [53].

Currently, there are no ready-to-use modules available to create DTs for any system, or reusable DTs capable of replicating all relationships within a system [52]. Without a general framework, it becomes difficult to apply a DT across different applications and systems uniformly, which complicates development and implementation.

DTs improve efficiency by reducing operational, development, and production times and errors. They streamline and facilitate system management. Additionally, they support smarter process design through simplified and reusable models and improve both quality and reliability in assembly and machining processes of satellite systems.
Fig. 5 conceptualizes DT value creation as a chain: mission & system context constrains DT design choices, which enable DT capabilities, producing measurable system outcomes.

In this review, most studies address exactly one lifecycle phase (40 out of 46), while only a small subset spans multiple phases (4 out of 46), and only two span all three phases. This matters because phase-local DTs typically yield local performance improvements, whereas lifecycle-spanning DTs enable digital thread continuity: requirements traceability, configuration management of models/data, and evidence accumulation across mission evolution.

The evidence base concentrates in simulation only (15/46) and lab prototype settings (19/46), with fewer operationaluse studies (9/46) and limited field-analogue validation (3/46). No studies in this corpus were coded as explicitly reporting a hardware-/software-in-the-loop (HIL/SIL) validation stage.

citations.quote: Research gaps. The reviewed literature highlights four main gaps. First, many DT implementations remain phase-local and do not support lifecycle continuity from design to operation. Second, validation under representative space conditions remains limited, especially for uncertain environments and delayed communication. Third, data availability and interoperability remain major barriers, particularly when proprietary design and production data are required. Fourth, reusable architectures and reporting standards are still missing, making it difficult to compare DT implementations across studies.
